## From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

### The Old-School View of Toughness
Traditional toughness is defined by perseverance, discipline, stoicism, and overcoming pain without showing weakness. College students and elite athletes alike describe it as playing through pain, exhibiting emotional fortitude, and showing no distress. This image often conjures a strong, brute male—a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in or the last NHL player without a helmet.

### Bobby Knight: Success Through Control and Abuse
Coach Bobby Knight’s 1976 Indiana basketball team went undefeated and won a national championship, which he attributed to toughness: “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” Yet his methods were abusive. He hung tampons in lockers of players he deemed “soft,” taped pictures of women’s genitalia in rooms, and unleashed profane tirades (e.g., “I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground…”). He once brought a piece of feces-covered toilet paper to show players what he thought of them, and was filmed choking a player. Knight’s version of toughness relied on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear to establish control—a model still pervasive today.

### Tough Parenting: The Authoritarian Style
Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind classified parenting styles by two dimensions: responsiveness (attunement to a child’s needs) and demandingness (expectations and control). Authoritarian parents are high in demandingness and low in responsiveness. They rely on fear, threats, and punishment; a typical refrain is “because I said so.” In one study, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” They jump to criticism after a mistake, ground children for subpar grades without support, and command boys to “suck it up, don’t cry.” 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. The problem is not expectations or punishment per se, but an extreme mismatch between demand and support. The same dynamic applies to coaching and leadership: we’ve emphasized demandingness while forgetting warmth, care, and responsiveness.

### Callousness and Machismo
Toughness language reveals a callous ideal: to harden, make insensitive, develop thick skin. We call teams “soft,” demand they “show no signs of weakness,” and use exercise as punishment to “toughen them up.” In youth sports, parents justify vomiting after workouts as necessary to find an “inner lacrosse warrior.” Toughness is tied to masculinity and machismo—told to “man up” or “stop being a pussy.” The image of toughness is The Rock or Vin Diesel, not a small female. Yet research shows women quietly handle pain better than men, and those who display external machismo are often the “weakest.”

### The Downfall of a Callous View
On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair collapsed during conditioning sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” It took 34 minutes to remove him from the field and another 28 minutes to call 911; he died of heatstroke two weeks later. Rhabdomyolysis, a once-rare condition where damaged muscle products leak into the bloodstream, has become more common due to extreme workouts designed to “test” athletes, not improve fitness. Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse, and risky behaviors. In sport, a controlling style is linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. Even in discipline, authoritarian parenting correlates with higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian homes coped worse with military challenges. This approach creates fragile, dependent individuals who act only to avoid punishment, not from internal drive.

### Redefining Toughness: Real vs. Fake
Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance. It’s Bobby Knight’s tantrums, the bully, the executive who masks insecurity by yelling, the coach who injures athletes. Real toughness is “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

Pete Carroll exemplifies real toughness. He allows players to be themselves, encourages meditation and yoga, and turns mistakes into positives. He wants players who come through when the game is on the line, but believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, and bouncing back—not solely discipline. Carroll’s “always compete” practices give players skills to handle adversity. Other successful coaches like Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni share this humanistic approach. A 2008 study of nearly 200 basketball players found that promoting mental toughness lies not in autocratic, authoritarian styles but in environments emphasizing “trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

### A Personal Search for Real Toughness
The author, a miler, recounts a race where he suddenly couldn’t breathe. His usual strategy of zoning out and then grinding through pain failed when his airway seemed to close. He collapsed, later diagnosed by Dr. Stephen Miles with paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—a reflex malfunction where vocal cords shut on inhalation, triggered by strong emotions and stress. His old “push until you puke” approach backfired, forcing him to learn to relax and keep his mind and body steady under maximum discomfort. This experience launched his search for a new model of toughness.

### The Four Pillars of Real Toughness
The book will cover four pillars:
- Pillar 1: Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
- Pillar 2: Listen to Your Body
- Pillar 3: Respond Instead of React
- Pillar 4: Transcend Discomfort

Real toughness is not bulldozing but navigating—sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting. It requires many tools, not just a hammer. The military, often seen as the epitome of macho toughness, has actually been perfecting this resilience model for decades. We took the drill sergeant but forgot the training and support.

**Toughness Maxim:** Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.

## The Basic Categories and Hard Edges

Being organized means that where something is matches what it means to you. The outer ring of the Workflow Diagram shows seven primary categories that must be kept pristinely distinct—visually, physically, and psychologically—to prevent psychological numbness: a Projects list, project support material, calendar actions and information, Next Actions lists, a Waiting For list, reference material, and a Someday/Maybe list. If categories blur (e.g., reference mixed with reading material, or calendar items on action lists), trust erodes and rethinking bogs you down. Once you have clarified what each item means, all you really need are lists and folders. A “list” can be a file folder of separate notes, a titled page, or a digital inventory.

## Organizing Action Reminders

### Calendar: The Hard Landscape
Only actions that must occur on a specific day or at a specific time belong on the calendar—the “hard landscape” around which other work is done. Resist the impulse to put “would like to do” items there; the calendar must be sacred territory, showing only true day- or time-specific commitments (e.g., “10:00–11:00 meet with Jim” or “Call Rachel Tuesday”).

### Context-Based Next-Action Lists
As-soon-as-possible actions are best organized by the context required to complete them—the tool, location, or situation. Common categories:

- **Calls**: All phone calls, with numbers recorded alongside each item so you can act in small windows of time.
- **At Computer**: Actions needing a computer. If connectivity matters, separate an “Online” list from offline computer work.
- **Errands**: Things to do when out and about (e.g., “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist”). Sublists (e.g., “hardware store” with attached items) are useful.
- **At Office**: Actions requiring physical presence at the office (e.g., purging a filing cabinet). For multiple locations, use “At Office A” and “At Office B.”
- **At Home**: Actions only doable at home (e.g., “Hang new watercolor print,” “Switch closets to winter clothes”).
- **Agendas**: Items to discuss with specific people or in standing meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, and regular meetings. Add ad hoc agendas quickly.
- **Read/Review**: Longer-than-two-minute reading. Use a physical stack tray or portable folder labeled “Read/Review.” For rigorous reading, a “Review/Respond” category may help. Digitally, a “Review/Watch” folder can hold links to videos or articles.

### Waiting For List
Track all deliverables or projects others are responsible for (e.g., tickets ordered, client OK on a proposal). Keep this list close to your Next Actions lists. Record the date requested and any agreed-upon due date—follow-up is more meaningful when you can say, “You’ve had the proposal now for three weeks.” Review it regularly to decide whether to check status or escalate.

### Using Originals as Action Reminders
Some paper and e-mail items serve as their own reminders. For paper: a “Bills to Pay” folder or “Receipts to Process” envelope can hold actionable documents, but only if you review them consistently. For e-mail: create an **@ACTION** folder for longer-than-two-minute actionable e‑mails and an **@WAITING FOR** folder for delegated items (cc or bcc yourself when delegating). This gets the inbox to empty—unread messages become true “in” to process. The danger is that offscreen digital reminders disappear; you must review @ACTION and paper Pending stacks as rigorously as any list.

## Organizing Project Reminders

### The Projects List and Its Value
A Projects list is a comprehensive index of every commitment requiring more than one action step—not a plan or priority-ordered list. Its value: (1) critical for control and focus, (2) alleviates subtle tensions from small things that morph into bigger ones, (3) serves as the linchpin of the Weekly Review, and (4) facilitates relationship management by making all commitments visible for negotiation.

### Uncovering Hidden Projects
Look in three areas: (1) current activities—calendar entries, action lists, and workspace artifacts (e.g., a conference call about a client request reveals a project “Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ”); (2) higher-horizon interests and commitments—professional roles, goals, strategic plans, personal aspirations; (3) current problems, process improvements, and creative opportunities—any complaint or frustration signals a potential project (e.g., “Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance”).

### Subsorting and Subprojects
Most people use one master list. Common subsorts: Personal/Professional, Delegated Projects, or specific types (e.g., “Projects—Presentations” for a speaker). For large projects with subprojects (e.g., “Move to Amsterdam” unpacked into fifteen subprojects), either list the major project and keep subpieces as support material, or list active independent subprojects separately. The key is reviewing all components regularly.

### Project Support Materials
Support materials are resources, not action reminders. Don’t use stacks or files to prompt action—that creates numbness. Instead, put the project on the Projects list, actions on action lists, and store plans, notes, and reference in support folders. For ad hoc project thinking, use attached notes in software, dedicated e‑mail folders (e.g., “Johnson Partnership—Active”), paper files, or notebook pages. Consistently extract next actions from these notes during reviews.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials
Reference requires no action—it’s your library. Distinguish it cleanly from actionable items. Systems include: general-reference filing (paper, e‑mail, simple digital storage), large-category filing for topics with 50+ folders, contact managers (purely data stores, not action reminders), and libraries/archives. Store based on when and where you’ll need access (mobile, briefcase, office, cloud). There is no perfect system; build it from real information you want to keep.

### Someday/Maybe and Future Triggers
A Someday/Maybe list holds projects you might want to reassess later (e.g., “Learn Spanish,” “Write a mystery novel”). Populate it from creative imaginings (hobbies, trips, skills) and by reassessing current projects—move optional ones here if they won’t get attention for months. Special-interest lists (books to read, wines to try) blend reference and Someday/Maybe. Avoid “Hold and Review” piles that are never reviewed; process them into appropriate categories.

Use the calendar for day-specific future triggers: (1) triggers for activating projects (e.g., when to add “Annual sales conference” to the Projects list), (2) events you might attend, (3) decision catalysts (e.g., “Hire/fire” or “Change job/career”) to revisit at a later date. It’s OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

### The Tickler File
A physical tickler file uses 43 folders—31 daily (1–31) and 12 monthly—to hold actual documents you want to see on a future date. Each day, empty that day’s folder into your in-tray and refile it at the back of the dailies (now representing the same day next month). It handles travel documents, birthday reminders, meeting agendas, and more. It demands checking daily; if you skip days, trust fails.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Checklists are “recipes of potential ingredients” for projects, procedures, events, and areas of responsibility. When fuzzy commitments arise (e.g., “Exercise more regularly,” “Maintain good morale on my team”), first identify inherent projects and next actions. For ongoing standards, create overview checklists of key areas (career goals, health, team morale, processes) to review regularly. The more novel the situation, the more external control you need—new roles or unfamiliar procedures demand checklists until they become automatic. Be ready to create ad hoc checklists for anything from “Core Life Values” to “Things to Take Camping.” As Alfred North Whitehead observed, “Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.”

## The Infomercial and the Universal Need for Hope

The chapter opens with a scenario: you’re on the couch at 2:00 a.m., passively watching TV, stuck in inertia. This state signals a crisis of hope. A charismatic infomercial host appears, claiming to solve all your problems and make all your dreams come true. He speaks to your pain by asserting that he once felt just as lost and hopeless, and that your suffering is not unique but universal—“I, too, once felt lost,” he says. “I felt alone, isolated, hopeless. I, too, used to lie awake at night for no particular reason, wondering if there was something wrong with me, wondering what was this invisible force standing between myself and my dreams.” This appeal works because everyone experiences the powerlessness and guilt inherent to existence, and in low moments, we despair. The host’s message bypasses your Thinking Brain and targets your Feeling Brain’s desperate need for hope and salvation. The infomercial is a metaphor for how religions—broadly defined—recruit followers by offering hope. The host’s outlandish claims become believable because the need for meaning beats down psychological defenses; he promises permanent fulfillment and eternal life, and the viewer, craving hope, signs up.

## The Three Pillars of Hope

Hope requires three components: values (a vision of a better future), self-control (a sense that you can reach that future), and community (others who share your values and support your efforts). When any of these are missing, hope collapses. Religions supply all three by providing a shared value system, rituals that reinforce a sense of agency, and a group identity. Young adulthood is a period when many struggle with all three—for the first time, they must decide who to be, manage their own behavior without constant oversight, and find a community to solidify their identity. This makes them prime targets for recruitment.

## The God Value and Types of Religions

Every person’s Feeling Brain adopts a highest value, called the “God Value,” through which all other values are interpreted. This God Value is always faith-based, because values are subjective and cannot be verified by evidence. Evidence belongs to the Thinking Brain; values are decided by the Feeling Brain. You can argue facts endlessly, but people interpret experiences through their God Value. For example, a meteorite hitting a town would be interpreted as divine punishment by a religious person, proof of no God by an atheist, a reason to party by a hedonist, and an investment opportunity by a capitalist. The only exception is when evidence itself becomes the God Value—the religion of science.

Religions are categorized by their God Value into three types:

- **Spiritual religions** draw hope from supernatural beliefs (e.g., Christianity, Islam, Buddhism). They are high risk/high reward, extremely resilient because their claims are unverifiable, and often encourage hope through an afterlife, making followers willing to die for them. They require the most skill and charisma to start but can last millennia. For most of history, when material improvement was impossible for the masses, the promise of an afterlife held society together.
- **Ideological religions** draw hope from this-worldly systems (e.g., capitalism, communism, environmentalism). They are partially verifiable but still rely on faith because many concepts (money, citizenship, ethnicity) are socially constructed. They are more common but face more competition and typically last decades rather than centuries. They play on “Normal Difficulty.” Bad ideologies like racism persist due to ignorance more than malice, because they offer some hope.
- **Interpersonal religions** draw hope from other people (e.g., romantic love, celebrity worship, sports fandom, political leaders). They are the most common and easiest to form, playing on “Easy” mode. Families function as mini-churches; romantic love can be a quasi-spiritual experience. Sports are a clear example: millions gather to watch arbitrary rules and deify or demonize athletes. Politics similarly deifies leaders. Modern civilization has weakened these small interpersonal tribes and replaced them with large ideological religions, making it easier for new religions to recruit followers by offering emotional attachment.

## Step One: Sell Hope to the Hopeless

The best recruits are those whose lives are at their worst, because when values fail, people grasp for new ones. All major religions historically sent missionaries to the poor and destitute. Jim Jones built his following from the homeless and marginalized; Jesus, Buddha, and Moses all preached to the downtrodden, promising them the kingdom of heaven as a “fuck you” to corrupt elites. Today, social media algorithms amplify extreme content, making it easier than ever to attract the hopeless.

The author recounts a 2005 encounter in Boston with the LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM), a far-left ideological religion founded by Lyndon LaRouche. Members held signs reading “America Deserved It” with images of 9/11, and pamphlets depicting Dick Cheney with devil horns and George W. Bush with a Hitler mustache. ## Kant’s Uncompromising Reason

Immanuel Kant rejected hope and its flawed human values, confronting the Uncomfortable Truth—that all value systems are ultimately arbitrary—with pure reason. He argued for a right and wrong transcending Feeling Brain judgments, lived uncompromisingly, and sought a moral system independent of any imagined future payoff. His rigid daily routine and immense intellectual output—from defending individual dignity to inspiring the UN and Einstein—reflected a mind that refused to accept the nihilistic implications of the abyss.

## How to Grow Up: From Child to Adolescent

Early development is driven by exploration. A child’s Feeling Brain collects pleasure/pain data, building a primitive value hierarchy: ice cream is good, hot stoves are bad. Identity is small and fragile, constituted solely by immediate pleasures and pains; the child is a little tyrant unable to empathize. The author’s own experience—touching a hot stove and gorging on stolen ice cream—illustrates how the child learns basic preferences and priorities.

This phase exhausts itself not because the world runs out, but because there is too much world to explore. The two brains shift to developing rules. After repeated encounters with flames, the child forms a rule that all flames are dangerous; after seeing Mom’s anger, she learns raiding the freezer is always bad. Abstract principles like fairness and prudence emerge—values that cannot be pointed to.

The adolescent no longer acts solely on pleasure/pain. She applies if/then rules, thinking through cause-and-effect chains, understanding that actions have consequences and desires must be negotiated with others and society’s rules. This is a cognitive leap: developing higher-level, abstract values for a wider range of contexts. The adolescent tries on different social roles—clothes, speech, music—to see what brings approval. However, the adolescent still sees everything as a trade-off, a calculated transaction made out of fear of negative repercussions: doing what the boss says for money, calling mother to avoid being yelled at, doing homework to not ruin the future. Nothing is done for its own sake; everything is a means to some pleasurable end. The adolescent is still a child at heart, just thinking a few moves ahead. This transactional approach is self-defeating because one never lives one’s own life, merely an aggregation of others’ desires.

## How to Be an Adult: Unconditional Principles

Most advice on being an adult focuses on rule- and transaction-based behaviors (job interviews, finances, cleaning), which are means to superficial ends. But the most important things—love, companionship, respect, trust—cannot be gained through bargaining. If you have to convince someone to love you, they don’t love you. Bargaining destroys these things; you cannot conspire for happiness.

Adulthood is realizing that some abstract principles are right and good for their own sake, even if they cause pain. An adolescent says she values honesty because it produces good results, but tells white lies when confronted. An adult is honest because honesty is more important than her own pleasure or pain, more important than getting what she wants. Honesty is an end, not a means. An adolescent’s love is an emotional swap meet; an adult loves freely without expecting return, because that is the only thing that makes love real. An adult gives without seeking return, because to do otherwise defeats the purpose of a gift.

These principled values are unconditional—ends in themselves. The difference between child, adolescent, and adult is not age or what they do, but why they do it. The child steals ice cream because it feels good, oblivious to consequences. The adolescent doesn’t steal because he knows it will create worse future consequences, a bargain with his future self. Only the adult doesn’t steal for the simple principle that stealing is wrong, and to steal, even if she gets away with it, would make her feel worse about herself. Adult behaviors—the boss who takes the fall, the mother who sacrifices her happiness, the friend who tells hard truths—are what hold the world together.

Children transcend pleasure/pain values by pursuing them and experiencing their failure. Stealing ice cream leads to Mom’s punishment, forcing the child to reckon with trade-offs. Good early parenting implements correct consequences: punish stealing, reward sitting quietly. Parents who coddle fail to teach that the world doesn’t cater to whims; the child later faces painful social punishment. Conversely, abused children receive random, cruel consequences that follow no logical pattern, so no higher values develop. Both coddled and abused children often remain stuck in childhood value systems.

Graduating to adolescence requires trust—the child must trust that behavior produces predictable outcomes. Without trust, no reliable principles form, and everything devolves back into childish selfishness. People get stuck in adolescence due to trauma or neglect. Bullying victims, for example, assume all affection must be hard-won through practiced actions; they become skilled manipulators, believing life is a high school gymnasium where you must shove others into lockers lest you be shoved first.

Adolescents need to be shown that bargaining is a never-ending treadmill and that real value is unconditional. This requires parents and teachers who demonstrate unconditionality by being unconditional themselves—trusting, respecting, loving without forcing it. When parents and teachers fail, it’s usually because they themselves are stuck at adolescent values, bargaining love for sex, loyalty for affection, respect for obedience. The transactional cycle replicates across generations. Making the leap to adulthood requires faith and the courage to abandon hope—to act unconditionally even if it brings pain.

Religions originally pushed people toward unconditional virtues, but they get co-opted by transactional adolescents and narcissistic children. Kant started from the observation that consciousness is the only scarce, unique thing in the universe—the only force that can reason, direct existence, and generate greater complexity. The most fundamental moral duty is the preservation and growth of consciousness, both in ourselves and in others. This single principle pulls people out of adolescent bargaining into adult virtue. Hope is fundamentally transactional—a bargain between present actions and an imagined pleasant future. Lying misleads another’s conscious behavior for your own goal; cheating violates others’ expectations for personal aims; violence treats another as a means to a political or personal end. ## The Uncomfortable Truth

### Witold Pilecki and the Limits of Hope

Witold Pilecki, a decorated Polish officer and father of two, volunteered in 1940 to be arrested and sent to Auschwitz—the only person known to have willingly entered a Nazi concentration camp. His initial mission was to organize a mutiny and break out imprisoned Polish soldiers. Once inside, he discovered a reality far worse than anyone suspected: prisoners were shot for fidgeting, worked to death on meaningless tasks, and a third of his barracks died in the first month. Despite this, Pilecki built an entire underground resistance unit with a chain of command, logistics, and communication to the outside world, using laundry baskets for messages and a homemade radio. His aim was a full-scale revolt.

Then the mass murder of Jews began. Pilecki’s reports to the Secret Polish Army became frantic: tens of thousands were being gassed daily, the death toll potentially in the millions. He begged for the camp to be liberated or at least bombed. His intelligence reached the Polish government-in-exile, then Allied Command, and eventually Eisenhower and Churchill. All assumed he was exaggerating. No help came. In 1943, Pilecki escaped by faking illness, cutting telephone wires, and sprinting to a river under fire.

After the war, he spied on the new Communist regime, documenting Soviet infiltration and atrocities. Warned of his impending arrest, he refused to flee, saying he would rather die Polish than live as something else. Captured in 1947, he was tortured for nearly a year—so severely that he told his wife “Auschwitz was just a trifle.” At his show trial in 1948, he declared: “I have tried to live my life such that in the hour of my death I would feel joy rather than fear.” He was executed. Pilecki’s heroism was not mere bravery but the ability to conjure hope where there is none, to hold an unshaken “Why?” even when everything is fucked.

### The Uncomfortable Truth and the Necessity of Hope

The Uncomfortable Truth is that one day you and everyone you love will die, and beyond a tiny group for a brief time, little you do will matter. The universe does not care about your mother’s hip replacement, your boss’s spreadsheet, or who wins an election. We are inconsequential cosmic dust. Our psyche cannot bear this meaninglessness directly; it needs hope like a fish needs water. Hope is the belief that the future can be better than the present and that we can navigate toward that improvement. Without hope, we spiritually die.

The opposite of happiness is not anger or sadness—those still mean you care. The opposite is hopelessness: a cold, bleak nihilism, the sense that nothing matters. Hopelessness is the root of anxiety (fear of a failed future), depression (belief in a meaningless future), addiction, and obsession. All are desperate attempts to generate hope. Therefore, the mind’s primary project is the construction of hope. All meaning we perceive is built to maintain it.

We construct “hope narratives”—before/after stories that give life purpose. The author describes how, after his grandfather’s death, he felt he must live to make his dead grandfather proud, even though they hadn’t been close and the idea was irrational. That narrative infused banal experiences with import and sustained him. Such narratives can be religious or secular: raising kids, saving the environment, making money, improving a golf swing. They all share the belief that (a) there is potential for growth or salvation, and (b) there are ways to get there. When people seek their “life’s purpose,” they are really asking what to hope for. Faith—religious or otherwise—protects against the Uncomfortable Truth; religious people suffer depression and suicide at lower rates.

### The Paradox of Progress

Materially, the world has never been better: extreme poverty, violence, illiteracy, and disease are at historic lows. Yet in rich, developed nations, hopelessness is spreading. This is the paradox of progress: the better things get, the more anxious and desperate we feel. Statistics bear this out: depression and anxiety among young people have risen for eighty years; adult depression has climbed for twenty years. Life satisfaction has dropped since 1985, stress has increased, drug overdoses are at an all-time high, and nearly half of Americans report feeling isolated or left out. Social trust is plummeting; by 2006, the most common number of close confidants was zero. Meanwhile, extremism, conspiracy theories, and prepper subcultures grow. The wealthier and safer the place, the higher the suicide rate.

Hope does not care about problems already solved; it cares only about the problems that remain. The better the world gets, the more we have to lose, and the less we feel we have to hope for. Hope is not based on statistics about the past but on visions of the future.

### The Three Pillars of Hope

To build and maintain hope, we need three things:

1. **A sense of control** – feeling we can affect our own fate.
2. **A belief in the value of something** – something important enough to strive for.
3. **A community** – a group that shares our values and works toward them.

Lose any one, and you lose the others; lose any, and you lose hope. The following chapters will examine how we develop control (chapter 2), values (chapter 3), and community (chapter 4), and then explore why, despite all progress, we feel worse.
